Adult Scardinius plotizza from Lake Skadar typically attain a fork length of 39 cm [Li = 39 cm], a measurement that positions them among the larger-bodied cyprinids endemic to the Balkan region and likely reflects the productive lacustrine conditions of their primary habitat. This ultimate size is achieved through a growth trajectory that begins with a remarkably small initial mass at the onset of exogenous feeding; newly hatched larvae emerge from eggs with an average diameter of roughly 1.54 mm, yielding a wet weight at birth of only 0.0019 grams [Wwb = 0.0019 grams]. Such a diminutive birth mass is consistent with the reproductive strategy typical of many r-selected freshwater teleosts that produce numerous, small offspring to offset high early-life mortality. The ontogenetic transition from this lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva to an actively feeding, free-swimming larva is a critical period during which the larvae must locate suitable zooplanktonic prey to sustain the rapid growth required to reach a size refuge from predation.

Sexual maturation in this species coincides with the attainment of a fork length of 16 cm [Lp = 16 cm], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. At this developmental milestone, individuals weigh approximately 48.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 48.6 grams], representing a substantial increase from the 0.0019 grams at birth and indicating that a considerable investment in somatic growth precedes reproductive competence. The time required to reach this pubertal length is influenced by local thermal conditions; in the temperate waters of Lake Skadar, this transition typically spans multiple growing seasons. Reaching puberty at a relatively modest size of 16 cm suggests that this species may adopt a bet-hedging strategy, initiating reproduction earlier than some congeners while still capable of continued growth toward the ultimate adult size of 39 cm. The ecological implication is that young adults may contribute to the next generation even under fluctuating environmental conditions that could truncate their lifespan.

Reproductive output for Scardinius plotizza has been characterized under controlled conditions at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], reflecting the typical summer spawning temperatures of its natural lake habitat. Field estimates derived from length-fecundity relationships for a closely related congener indicate that a female of the species can produce up to approximately 384 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 384 eggs per day] during the peak spawning period. This daily fecundity, sustained over the course of a spawning season that may extend for several weeks, underscores the high reproductive potential of this iteroparous cyprinid. The relationship is strongly size-dependent, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the total egg production of the population, an observation consistent with the positive allometry between body size and fecundity documented in many freshwater fishes. The ability to maintain this rate of gamete output is contingent upon adequate nutritional reserves and favorable thermal regimes.

As individuals approach their asymptotic size, the maximum recorded body mass for Scardinius plotizza reaches 661 grams [Wwi = 661 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions that describe the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of the species. This ultimate wet weight represents a nearly 350,000-fold increase from the wet weight at birth of 0.0019 grams, a staggering ontogenetic scaling of body size that is typical of teleosts with indeterminate growth. The relationship between length and mass follows a cubic power function, meaning that the heaviest individuals—those approaching 39 cm—are not merely longer but disproportionately more massive due to the volumetric increase in muscle and viscera. Such a high ultimate mass likely confers advantages in fecundity and competitive dominance, although it also entails greater absolute metabolic demands. The documented 661-gram ceiling provides a useful benchmark for comparative studies of cyprinid life-history evolution across the Adriatic basin.

The maximum lifespan of Scardinius plotizza has been estimated at 11 years [am = 11 years] in the wild, based on scale and otolith annuli readings from the Lake Skadar population at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This longevity, when considered alongside the ultimate fork length of 39 cm, paints a picture of a moderately slow-lived species among cyprinids, one that invests in prolonged somatic growth before and even after the onset of reproduction at the 16 cm fork length threshold. Maintaining such a lifespan requires the fish to survive multiple spawning seasons and to cope with seasonal fluctuations in food availability and temperature, particularly during winter periods when metabolic rates slow. The maximum reported age of 11 years [am = 11 years] was recorded in a population experiencing stable water temperatures near 22 °C [T = 22 °C] during the active growing season, conditions that favor consistent annual growth increments. In less productive or more thermally variable habitats, longevity may be somewhat reduced, highlighting the role of environmental stability in shaping the realized lifespan of this species.
